Question: In the EPR paper, did Einstein demonstrate a better understanding of QM than Bohr?
Answer: It shows that Einstein had a very deep understanding of quantum theory. Einstein was convinced that quantum theory was incomplete, and used the EPR thought experiment to show this. However, there was a caveat. Einstein had assumed a property called local realism. This is quite reasonable, given his understanding of relativity and how it solved Newton's action at a distance problem with gravity. However, John Bell sought a way to test local realism. He developed a theorem that specified that no theory based on local realism could reproduce all the results of quantum theory. He specifically developed a quantitative test using the correlations observed between entangled particles. This was different to the EPR experiment because EPR considered continuous variables, while Bell considered discrete two state variables that greatly simplified the experiment. The result is a violation of Bell's inequality. The violation means that the assumption of local realism cannot be supported, while quantum theory successfully describes the observed correlations. This effectively rules out local realism as being a characteristic of reality and means that Einstein’s assumption in the EPR paper was wrong. Although, this should not detract from Einstein's insight on this matter. Bell's work was published nearly a decade after Einstein's death, and the first experiments of Clauser almost a decade later again. The matter was essentially closed in 2015, and a Nobel prize awarded in 2022. All of this was inspired by Einstein’s insight. So rather than proclaim that Einstein was wrong, it is more fitting to see the journey that he inspired that culminated in the work being awarded a Nobel prize nearly 90 years later. In fact, the EPR paper is still widely cited today, and is Einstein's most cited paper. In contrast, Bohr is the father of the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum theory. Bohr's approach was more akin to embracing the mystery of quantum theory, which is essentially the shutup and calculate approach. While widely taught as a matter of practicality, it embraces measurement as something metaphysical. I don't think Einstein was comfortable with this. Indeed, many physicists are still uncomfortable with this. Therefore, I'd argue that this does not constitute a better understanding of quantum theory. Rather, just acceptance because it seems to work. That's why I hold that the EPR paper is rather more important, because it has led us in directions that have culminated in a far better understanding of quantum theory.

Question: Why do quantum physics and Einstein's theory of relativity seem so counterintuitive compared to classical physics?
Answer: I suspect that is stems from our intuition, which is based on reinforcement learning (we experience things happening and learn from that). Clearly, this is a very powerful way of general learning. However, with our skills at higher reasoning, we started probing our intuitive model of reality and found some alarming consequences. This was evident with the ancient Greeks who discovered the concept of infinity, or the infinitesimal. This gave us the concept of there being a fundamental indivisible part called the atom. What was remarkable about this is that such a conclusion was reached thousands of years before the discovery of the atom. Of course, we now know that atoms are not fundamental. Nevertheless, that the very concept of a fundamental particle was developed by the ancient Greeks is absolutely remarkable. This concept alone already clashes with our intuition. What is such a particle made from? This question has no answer, yet many people still demand one. The only question you can ask about fundamental particles is, what are its properties? Yet people ask, what is the size of a fundamental particle, as if it were an object like an apple. Its difficult to understand that such questions don't really make sense. The theory of special relativity is similarly seemingly nonsensical. There seems to be no end to velocity addition. Yet, the speed of light seems to impose such a limit. Why? The answer is not so simple. Velocity addition still works, but in a space-time with a slightly different symmetry. The speed of light is not a simple speed limit. It was Hermann Minkowski who worked out why such strange space-time symmetry was a reasonable assumption, and that is because the speed of light actually represents the speed of causality. While space and time are relative, the causal ordering of events should be absolute. That means that any observer travelling at any relative speed should agree with the causal ordering of events if such events are causally connected. In other words, space and time are relative in order for causal ordering to be absolute. How do we arrive at such a conclusion by just experiencing the world around us? The speed of light is so fast that it appears to be effectively infinite to us. Similarly, general relativity was derived from a few simple considerations; that Newton's first law could be extended to the more general case of accelerated motion, or that motion not under the influence of any external force should be considered natural. When Einstein reasoned that a person falling from a roof would experience no external forces while falling, he considered this to be the natural state of motion. When combined with the fact that gravity is universally attractive, the geometrical theory of gravity was born. That took a lot of brain power and painstaking persistence to develop. The mathematics is so advanced that it is very difficult to convey the intricacies of this theory to anyone who hasn't studied it. The bottom line is that if we are sufficiently observant, we could reach the deductions that have culminated in these theories. This is what experiments are designed to do. In all the aforementioned theories, experiments have played a crucial role in the development of the theory. Classical physics, by contrast, is a collection of common sense ideas that are not in any sense unified. Particles and waves involve separate theories that must be somehow pasted together. This was done most successfully in Maxwell's equations of electromagnetism. Ironically, this set of equations actually predicted the same space-time symmetry as special relativity. Yet this is supposedly a classical theory. Furthermore, the theory could not explain the curious property of the double slit experiment with low light levels. It was the failure of classical theories to describe a range of experimental phenomena that actually led to the development of modern physics. Therefore, our modern theories do not jibe with common sense. Yet like the Greeks proposing the atom, we have used our higher faculties to reveal where common sense falters and have new theories that better fit with all observed phenomena.

Question: What is the belief behind the connection between quantum mechanics and consciousness?
Answer: This is due to the measurement problem. In short, standard quantum mechanics is not a complete physical theory. This is where consciousness sneaks in. In essence, quantum mechanics is a two-part theory. The first part is purely physical, and gives the deterministic evolution of the wavefunction due to the various interactions of the constituent parts. This evolution is completely causal and time reversible. This part of the theory has been remarkably successful. It gives us the structure of the atom, for example. However, everything is treated in terms of a wavefunction, which is not observable. In other words, the purely physical theory has some deficiencies. What we would like is for a theory to predict measurement outcomes. This is why there is a second part to the theory. This included a means of interpreting the wavefunction as a device for calculating a probability density (via the Born rule), and then the conversion of a probability to an actuality (the collapse of the wavefunction) on measurement. This is the formalism of quantum mechanics. The problem rests with the seemingly innocuous word, “measurement”. Just what constitutes a measurement? This is where there has been some vigorous debate, which is known as the measurement problem. I believe it was John von Neumann that first considered consciousness as a requisite part of the measurement. He considered measurement to be a purely physical process, as modelled by the first part of the theory, and at some point in the interaction chain one needed to make a cut at the point where the measurement actually occurs. This was called the von Neumann cut. The problem is that the theory gives no clue as to where the cut should be made. It is completely arbitrary. Eugene Wigner took this a step further in proposing the Wigner's friend paradox. That's where Wigner's friend makes a measurement of a quantum system, collapsing the wavefunction, while Wigner considers his friend to be entangled with the quantum system and can prove this by demonstrating quantum interference of the combined friend-quantum system. So did his friend really collapse the wavefunction? The Wigner's friend paradox uses the friend to make a measurement. This is important because we would all agree that we can make measurements. But who or what else can make a measurement? Can a rock make a measurement? Can an amoeba make a measurement? The problem with the concept of a measurement was outlined by John Bell in his 1991 Physics World article titled, 'Against measurement’. Therein he makes it very clear that quantum mechanics is not a complete physical theory due to the measurement problem. Mind you, in 1991 decoherence theory had long been established. Bell was adamant that this did not solve the measurement problem as some claim. Thus we are left with the Wigner's friend paradox as a crucial thought experiment that considers the reality of the measurement. Caslav Brukner considered combining the Wigner's friend experiment with a Bell test using entangled photon pairs. This was dubbed an extended Wigner's friend experiment from which he derived a no-go theorem similar to Bell's theorem. This work has been extended by Cavilcanti and Wiseman to produce the Local Friendliness theorem, which is an extension of Bell's theorem, and provides an inequality similar to, but more general than Bell's inequality. This includes the addition of a measurement objectivity axiom. To experimentally test the Local Friendliness inequality, one needs to use a suitable “friend”, which is some system that we can actually agree makes a measurement. This is where consciousness, or sentience is required. Finally, I'd like to simply illustrate why measurements are not purely physical. Consider a measurement of the height of an object. You place a measuring stick next to the object and note some number as indicated on the stick. The only physical part of this procedure is the placement of the stick. Yet we should agree that the measurement is more than just the placement of the stick. The measurement is the meaning we extract from the process. Ultimately, the Local Friendliness theorem indicates that it should be possible to find a fully physical theory that doesn't require the ambiguity of consciousness. In other words, the role of consciousness is an indication of the deficiency of quantum mechanics as a physical theory.

Question: Classical physics has shown that objects move because they were pushed by forces. Quantum physics has shown that objects move due to forces. What is difference?
Answer: I can't say that I understand this question. Newton's laws of motion identify inertial motion, which is straight line motion with constant velocity in the absence of an external force. Therefore, any deviation of this motion involves a force according to this definition. This first law identifies momentum as being the property that remains constant in the absence of a force. Using the second and third laws of motion, we can analyse the dynamics of a body. This is the most fundamental definition of a physical property (momentum) and the cause for a change in momentum (force). In essence, these are the cogs that we use to explain how the universe works. Newton's laws are considered to be just a part of a broader body of knowledge referred to as classical mechanics. There are many other formulations of classical mechanics that are easier to work with when considering complex systems, such as Hamiltonian and Lagrangian mechanics. The aforementioned alternatives work with energies rather than forces. As energy is a scalar quantity, these formulations are often much simpler. Therefore instead of forces, interactions between particles are represented by energies, referred to as interaction energies. The forces can be derived from the change in interaction energy, so there is no fundamental difference between the various approaches. Quantum theory can be obtained from the Hamiltonian formalism using what is called canonical quantization. This is not the only way to arrive at quantum theory. Another possibily more intuitive approach is to introduce Planck's constant into the Fourier transform. In doing this, one makes explicit use of the de Broglie matter-wave hypothesis, which is that massive particles have an associated wavelength. In working with the Fourier transform, one has immediately moved from a classical particle perspective to a wave perspective. So you would expect things to get a little strange. In particular, the so-called particle is now something far more abstract. It is represented by a wavefunction, which is generally distributed throughout space. However, what hasn't changed appreciably is the Hamiltonian. The Hamiltonian contains all the interaction energy terms, which essentially determine the forces. The salient difference is that the Hamiltonian is expressed using quantum operators, rather than simple real-valued variables. Therefore, the classical dynamics expressed using real-valued variables is instead represented by quantum operators acting on a wavefunction. However, the form of the Hamiltonian stays essentially the same. In other words, the forces are still there, but they now act to evolve a wavefunction rather than a point particle. This is a substantial difference, but the physics of the interactions remains the same. To go much further would require actually presenting a course on quantum theory…
